supplementary_news.content_title: Global trust in science lower than before Covid pandemic, report finds
supplementary_news.content: The proportion of people expressing at least some trust in science has fallen 5 per cent since 2018 Global trust in science is lower than it was before the Covid-19 pandemic, a new report has found. More than 140,000 people in 140 countries were polled for the third wave of The Wellcome Global Monitor, the world’s largest study into how people regard and feel about science. The proportion of people expressing at least some trust in science was 77 per cent in 2018, rose to 80 per cent in 2020, but then fell to 72 per cent in 2025. People who felt worse off financially, or had less confidence in their countries’ healthcare systems, were also less likely to say they trusted science. Only 21 per cent of respondents in sub-Saharan Africa reported having “a lot” of trust in science, compared with 54 per cent in Western Europe. Low trust levels are likely to have an impact on how health programmes can operate, experts said. “Public trust shapes whether scientific advances can make a meaningful difference in people’s lives,” said John-Arne Røttingen, CEO of Wellcome. “As the world faces increasing challenges, from infectious diseases to climate change and mental health, science has the potential for shaping a healthier future, but only if people trust that it is a force for good.” Despite the global bump in trust during the Covid-19 pandemic, in sub-Saharan Africa as well as Central Asia and Western Asia, there was a steady fall in trust across the three survey waves. And while in Central Asia the trend reflected a gradual softening of views, with more people moving from “a lot” of trust in science to “some” trust, in the other two regions views appeared to harden, with growing proportions saying they trust science either “not much” or “not at all”. A health worker collects a swab sample from a passenger to test for the Covid-19 coronavirus, on arrival at Anna International Airport in Chennai on December 24, 2022. (AFP/Getty) While there was some diversity between countries, overall only 28 per cent of respondents in sub-Saharan Africa felt science benefited “most” people in their country. “Across Africa, people have lived through a series of major shocks and challenges in recent years: rising living costs and economic insecurity, the lasting impacts of Covid-19, rising pressure on health systems, recurring disease outbreaks including mpox, Marburg virus and Ebola , conflict and displacement, and the growing effects of climate change on health,” said Dr Aneesa Ahmed, head of programmes at health NGO Amref Health Africa. “If families are struggling financially, if clinics lack medicines or staff, or if communities feel excluded from decision-making, trust can be affected.” Trust is, however, “fundamental” to health programmes, she said. “Communities may only encounter science through practical experiences such as an immunisation drive, a maternal health outreach clinic, or a local community health worker visit to their home. If people have low trust in the institutions delivering those services, or do not feel that programmes reflect their own priorities and realities, implementation becomes much harder.” The report comes as health systems in many African countries are reeling from the impact of aid cuts by countries like the US and UK, who have historically been major donors. Low trust also helped misinformation to spread, Ahmed added, “especially through social media”. Health authorities working to tackle the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) have frequently warned that mistrust and misinformation in local communities is hampering the response. In the DRC, 22 per cent of people reported having “no trust” in science at all. Dr Evelyn Gitau, chief scientific officer, Science for Africa Foundation and part of the report’s steering group, said that poor availability of laboratory tests early in the DRC outbreak had driven that mistrust. “All the interventions that we said would work, were not readily available,” she said, and so while “people knew what they were supposed to do [...] they rejected it because they felt things were taking too long”. She said there were wider issues where people in Africa were not feeling the benefits of research, even in communities that had been part of programmes for decades. “Trust in science is shaped by people’s lived experiences, including whether they can access and benefit from the systems and knowledge that science produces. In Africa, that means asking where research comes from, who leads and funds it, and whether local communities and institutions have ownership of, and benefit from, its results,” she added. “A lot of research, especially health research, has come to Africa, but it has come to Africa more from a north-south kind of gaze, so it’s research for the participants and not necessarily with them.” The fact most scientific research projects were health focused meant that “if our health systems are poor, people are going to really equate that to the fact that science is actually not working for them - and that is the reality, a lot of our health systems are really struggling,” she added. Playing in :00 shares Share this Article Share Share via device FacebookXLinkedInWhatsAppRedditEmailCopy Link Staff view 0 shares Comments Hawaiʻi Department of Health encourages residents to take common-sense precautions against influenza, COVID-19 and other respiratory viruses as respiratory virus activity increases throughout the state. Recent surveillance shows influenza activity increased, with 20.3% of specimens testing positive for flu during the week of Sept. 23-30, up from the previous week. The state Health Department also continues to monitor COVID-19 and reports cases began to decrease during the same week. Omicron variant of COVID-19. (File Image: World Health Organization) “Respiratory viruses circulate year-round in Hawaiʻi and we are seeing increased activity as we enter the fall respiratory virus season,” said State Epidemiologist Dr. Sarah Kemble. “Getting recommended vaccines, staying home when you are sick and taking simple precautions around others can help reduce the spread of illness and protect people who are more vulnerable to severe disease.” The West Coast Health Alliance, which includes Hawaiʻi, recently issued its 2026-27 respiratory virus season immunization recommendations. Alliance officials recommend annual flu vaccination for everyone 6 months and older, as well as updated COVID vaccination for specific higher risk populations, including all children ages 6 to 23 months, all adults age 65 years and older and people ages 2 to 64 years with risk factors. West Coast Health Alliance also recommends COVID vaccination for people planning pregnancy, are pregnant or postpartum; for healthcare workers; and other people living or working closely with people at higher risk, and anyone else who chooses vaccination to reduce the risk of severe illness. “People should talk with their healthcare provider about which vaccines are recommended for them and whether they are up to date,” Kemble said. “The updated vaccines are an important tool for reducing the risk of severe illness, particularly for people at higher risk.” State health officials also recommend several straightforward steps to help prevent respiratory illness: Stay home when sick. Stay home until you are fever-free at least 24 hours without using fever-reducing medication and other symptoms are mild and improving. Consider wearing a mask. Masks can provide additional protection, particularly in crowded indoor settings, when respiratory virus activity is high or when spending time around people at higher risk of severe illness. Improve indoor air. Open doors or windows, use air purifiers or gather outdoors when possible. Practice good hygiene. Wash hands regularly and cover coughs and sneezes. Test and seek treatment when appropriate. People at higher risk for severe disease who develop respiratory symptoms should contact their healthcare provider. Antiviral medications for COVID-19 and influenza work best when started as soon as possible. People at increased risk for severe respiratory illness include kūpuna, young children, pregnant people, people with weakened immune systems and people with certain underlying medical conditions. People who live with or regularly care for someone at higher risk can also take additional precautions to reduce the likelihood of spreading illness. Screenshot of image from Hawaiʻi Department of Health email. The state Health Department encourages residents to talk with their healthcare provider about individual vaccination needs and use reliable health information as respiratory virus activity changes. Visit the Hawaiʻi Department of Health respiratory virus resources website for more information about respiratory viruses, COVID-19, influenza and vaccination recommendations. supplementary_news.content: Catherine Mackinlay Updated Fri, October 9, 2026 at 4:05 PM UTC 0 Health officials have issued an update on the BA.3.2 'Cicada' Covid variant as infections rise (Image: Adam Gerrard / Daily Mirror) The Government has issued an update on a Covid variant dubbed "Cicada" as coronavirus infections rise across the UK. The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) said BA.3.2, sometimes referred to as the "Cicada" variant, is a highly divergent descendant of the Omicron BA.3 lineage which re-emerged in South Africa in late 2024. The strain has since been detected sporadically across multiple continents and has been designated a Variant Under Monitoring by the World Health Organisation (WHO). However, health officials stressed that the current public health risk from BA.3.2 is considered low, with no evidence that it causes increased severity, hospitalisation or mortality, although available evidence remains limited. The update comes as another Covid strain, XFG, remains the most common variant currently circulating. XFG, also known as Stratus and dubbed 'American Covid' in some media reports, has been circulating in the UK and elsewhere for around a year. UKHSA data shows Covid positive test rates rose to around seven per cent in September, while hospital admission rates increased by approximately 50 per cent over the same period. The increases have been recorded across England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, as well as elsewhere in Europe and the United States. Despite the rise, UKHSA said current data does not indicate that circulating variants are causing more severe illness than other Covid variants. Officials said increases in hospitalisations are broadly in line with the overall rise in Covid circulation, suggesting greater levels of infection rather than a particular variant causing more serious disease. UKHSA said several factors could be contributing to the current increase. Colder and wetter weather means people are spending more time indoors, making it easier for respiratory viruses to spread. It has also been roughly a year since the last significant Covid wave, meaning immunity from previous infections and vaccinations may be waning among parts of the population. People experiencing symptoms of a respiratory infection who have a high temperature or do not feel well enough to carry out their normal activities are advised to stay at home where possible and avoid contact with vulnerable people. The 'Cicada' variant re-emerged in South Africa in late 2024 (Image: Getty) Those who cannot stay at home are advised to wear a well-fitting face covering, avoid crowded or poorly ventilated places and practise good hand and respiratory hygiene. The NHS says Covid symptoms can include a high temperature, cough, shortness of breath, tiredness, headache, sore throat and a blocked or runny nose. UKHSA also stressed that vaccines remain the best defence against severe Covid illness and hospitalisation. People aged 75 and over, those with weakened immune systems and residents of care homes for older people are currently among those eligible for vaccination. UKHSA said it continues to monitor Covid variants using GP appointments, A&E attendances, hospitalisations and genomic sequencing. Hospital data helps officials track more severe cases and assess how quickly different variants are spreading. The agency also publishes weekly surveillance data on Covid and other respiratory illnesses throughout winter. People at the highest risk of becoming seriously ill may be eligible for NHS treatment if they develop symptoms and test positive. This can include people with weakened immune systems, certain cancers, kidney or liver disease and organ transplants. Some people with conditions affecting the lungs, brain or nervous system may also be eligible for treatment

Close Search & Section Navigation News UKUSAsiaFeature Business Entertainment Culture Sports Lifestyle Features National Trust Awards ACTAsAsian Business AwardsEastern Eye Property AwardsEastern Eye Restaurant Awards Trending Power List More ColumnComment More TrendingPower ListColumnComment Follow Us: Home> Lifestyle> Health> XFG 'American Covid" is rising in the UK: What you need to know> Submit Guest Post XFG 'American Covid" is rising in the UK: What you need to know XFG, also known as “Stratus,” is driving a rise in COVID activity across the UK, but health officials say there is no evidence it causes more severe illness. Here’s what the latest numbers, symptoms and vaccine guidance mean. That increase is worth watching, particularly as winter approaches and respiratory viruses generally circulate more widely. iStock By Vibhuti PathakOct 08, 2026 Vibhuti Pathak See Full Bio Highlights: FG is now a major COVID variant in the UK. UK COVID cases and hospital admissions are rising. There is no evidence XFG causes more severe disease. Symptoms remain similar to previous COVID variants. Health officials say there is no need for public panic. COVID-19 is once again making headlines in the UK, with infections and hospital admissions moving upward as autumn sets in. But for most people, the latest rise is a reason to be sensible, not scared. The XFG variant, sometimes called “Stratus” in media reports, is now one of the main SARS-CoV-2 lineages being tracked in the UK and globally. The World Health Organization classifies XFG as a variant under monitoring, while UKHSA says current evidence does not indicate that XFG causes more severe illness than other variants currently circulating. That is an important distinction as social media discussions about a new COVID “strain” can make a rise in cases sound more alarming than the evidence suggests. So, what is XFG? Ask AIHow does the rise of the XFG variant impact British Asian communities, especially those with higher risk factors? XFG is a descendant of the Omicron family of COVID-19 variants. It has become increasingly widespread internationally, with WHO data showing that it accounted for 49% of submitted SARS-CoV-2 sequences globally in the week ending August 23, 2026. Its growing prevalence is one reason health authorities continue to monitor it closely. But being widespread does not automatically mean being more dangerous. UKHSA's assessment remains reassuring: current data do not show that XFG or other currently common variants result in more severe disease. Why are UK cases rising? The latest UKHSA dashboard shows reported COVID cases reaching 1,364 in the seven days to September 23, an increase of 28.6 per cent from the previous seven-day period. Hospital admissions were also rising, reaching 261 in the week to August 31, up 15 per cent. That increase is worth watching, particularly as winter approaches and respiratory viruses generally circulate more widely. But health officials also point out that surveillance figures do not represent every COVID infection. Many people with mild symptoms may never seek medical attention or receive a formal diagnosis. So a rise in reported cases should not be interpreted as evidence that the country is heading back to the conditions seen during the early pandemic. What are healthcare experts saying? The message from public health authorities is essentially: keep an eye on the numbers, but don't panic. Alex Allen, a consultant epidemiologist at UKHSA, previously said that while COVID activity had shown increases, cases remained at low levels in the UK and that the agency was continuing to monitor variants in Britain and overseas. UKHSA's current assessment is similarly measured. Its experts say there is currently no indication that XFG causes more severe illness than other circulating variants. That means the most important question is not simply whether someone has XFG, but whether they are becoming seriously unwell or belong to a group at higher risk of complications. What symptoms should you look for? There is no confirmed symptom that uniquely identifies XFG. The NHS lists common COVID symptoms, including a high temperature, continuous cough, sore throat, blocked or runny nose, tiredness, headache, body aches and shortness of breath. Loss or change of smell or taste can also occur, although it is less characteristic of newer Omicron-lineage infections. Because these symptoms overlap with flu and ordinary respiratory infections, symptoms alone cannot reliably tell you which virus you have. Who needs to be more careful? COVID remains more concerning for older people, immunosuppressed people and others at increased risk of severe disease. The UK's autumn 2026 vaccination programme is specifically targeted at people at highest risk: adults aged 75 and over, residents of older-adult care homes and people aged six months and over who are immunosuppressed. The NHS says vaccination continues to provide protection against severe illness and hospitalisation. For eligible people, the latest UK programme includes an updated XFG-targeted Moderna vaccine for adults and an XFG-targeted Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine for eligible 12- to 17-year-olds. What should you do if you get symptoms? For most otherwise healthy people, the advice is straightforward: rest, drink plenty of fluids and stay home if you have a high temperature or feel too unwell to carry out normal activities. The NHS recommends avoiding contact with other people while you are unwell and taking particular care around people who are more vulnerable to serious infection. People eligible for COVID treatments because they are at particularly high risk should test promptly after developing symptoms, because antiviral treatment needs to be started quickly to be effective. Seek urgent medical advice through NHS 111 if symptoms are worsening or you are concerned. Call 999 or go to A&E for severe breathing difficulty, sudden chest pain, coughing up blood, collapse or other signs of a serious emergency. XFG is spreading, and UK COVID activity is rising. Those developments deserve monitoring, particularly heading into winter. But there is currently no evidence that XFG is a more severe form of COVID, and the UK remains far removed from the extraordinary hospitalisation levels seen during the pandemic's worst periods. UKHSA continues to monitor the variant, while the NHS is focusing vaccination on people most likely to suffer serious complications. For the public, the message is simple: stay informed, know the symptoms, protect vulnerable people around you and take up vaccination if you are eligible but there is no need to panic. american covidcoronavirus ukcovid symptoms 2026covid vaccine ukcovid variant ukcovid winter 2026covid-19 uknhs covid advicerespiratory viruses ukstratus coviduk covid cases 2026uk covid hospital admissionsuk covid vaccinationukhsa covidxfg covid ukxfg covid variantxfg omicronxfg symptomsxfg vaccinexfg variant symptomsxfg covid variant uk Add EasternEye As Your Trusted Source Related News Fitness Why Do Energy Crashes Happen During Workouts? supplementary_news.content: Home News Screeners Insights ScanXNewsSunshine Biopharma publishes study on MR1-114 efficacy Sunshine Biopharma publishes study on MR1-114 efficacy 1 min read | Published on 20 Jul 2026, 10:35 PM |Updated on 20 Jul 2026, 10:35 PM Reviewed by Riya DScanX News Team Add as a preferred source on Google Key Highlights Sunshine Biopharma Inc. and the University of Arizona published research in the Journal of Medicinal Chemistry on MR1-114, a PLpro inhibitor showing nanomolar potency against SARS-CoV-2 variants. The study demonstrated that MR1-114 matched Nirmatrelvir's efficacy in mouse models, suppressing viral replication and preventing weight loss. The compound targets the BL2 groove and cryptic Val70Ub pocket, offering a promising new therapeutic strategy. powered by *this image is generated using AI for illustrative purposes only. Sunshine Biopharma Inc. and the University of Arizona have published new research findings in the Journal of Medicinal Chemistry detailing the efficacy of MR1-114, a novel PLpro inhibitor, against SARS-CoV-2 variants. The study demonstrates that MR1-114 exhibits nanomolar potency in vitro against at least three variants of the virus, including the original Washington Strain, Delta, and Omicron BA.5. In vivo results from a mouse model of SARS-CoV-2 infection indicate that repeated oral administration of MR1-114 significantly suppressed pulmonary viral replication and prevented disease-associated weight loss, matching the therapeutic efficacy of Nirmatrelvir. The research highlights MR1-114's broad-spectrum activity and desirable ADME profile, including high oral bioavailability and preferential enrichment in the lungs of mice and rats. The compound targets two vulnerabilities remote from the catalytic site of the PLpro protease: the BL2 groove and the cryptic Val70Ub pocket. This approach addresses the challenge posed by PLpro's featureless active site, which has historically hindered the development of effective inhibitors. Dr. Rui Xiong, assistant professor in the Department of Pharmacology & Toxicology, noted that MR1-114 and its analogs offer a promising new strategy for targeting PLpro and could complement existing SARS-CoV-2 antivirals. OffOn Stream on WHO says suspected hantavirus cluster 'is not the start of a COVID pandemic' There are 12 suspected cases so far. ByMary Kekatos and Zoe Magee May 7, 2026, 4:39 PM An epidemiologist from the World Health Organization (WHO) said Thursday that the suspected hantavirus cluster aboard a cruise ship is not the beginning of another COVID-19 pandemic. Eight cases are currently being reported by the WHO, including five laboratory-confirmed cases and three suspected cases. Of those eight cases, three have died. Dr. Maria Van Kerkhove, an infectious disease epidemiologist and acting director of epidemic and pandemic management at the WHO, was asked during a press conference what the difference was between this cluster and the early days of the COVID pandemic. Related Officials in Arizona, Georgia monitoring some hantavirus cruise ship passengers who have returned to US "I want to be unequivocal here. This is not SARS-CoV-2. This is not the start of a COVID pandemic. This is an outbreak that we see on a ship," Van Kerkhove said. Van Kerkhove explained that hantavirus doesn't spread in the same way that coronaviruses do, but rather through "close, intimate contact." Most hantaviruses don't transmit from person to person. "The actions that are being taken on board [the ship] are precautionary to prevent any onward spread," she added. Health personnel assisting patients onto a boat from the cruise ship MV Hondius, while stationary off the port of Praia, the capital of Cape Verde, May 6, 2026. AFP via Getty Images There appears to be two confirmed cases and four suspected cases that have not been added to the WHO's official count yet. The Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport confirmed that two patients infected with the virus are currently hospitalized in the Netherlands, one at Radboud University Medical Center and the other at Leiden University Medical Center. Additionally, two Singapore residents who were on board the ship are currently being monitored. Singapore's Communicable Diseases Agency said it was notified of the individuals on May 4 and 5. "They have been isolated at the National Centre for Infectious Diseases, where they are being tested for hantavirus. The risk to the general public in Singapore is currently low," the agency said. The agency added that test results are pending, with one resident having a runny nose. The other is asymptomatic. The French Health Ministry also issued a statement on Thursday that a French national has been tested after they displayed mild symptoms. This person had been in contact with one of the confirmed cases. Related 3 people waiting to be medically evacuated from cruise ship at center of suspected hantavirus outbreak Three deaths have been recorded so far, including a married Dutch couple. The 70-year-old male patient died on April 11, and his body was taken off the ship on the island of St. Helena on April 24. His 69-year-old wife disembarked on the same day, and her health rapidly deteriorated. She died at a South Africa hospital on April 26. A third passenger, a German woman, presented with pneumonia symptoms starting on April 28, according to the WHO. The woman died on May 2 from causes not yet known, according to Oceanwide Expeditions, which operates the cruise ship. The WHO said 29 people disembarked on St. Helena on the same day that the body of the Dutch male patient and his wife disembarked. They traveled to 12 countries: Canada, Switzerland, Germany, Denmark, Great Britain, St. Kitts and Nevis, Netherlands, New Zealand, Singapore, Sweden, Turkey and the United States. Popular Reads Hurricane Isaias: At least 4 dead as Isaias downgraded 19 hours ago Fort Hood survivors speak out on Pentagon's decision to livestream Hasan's execution 2 days ago Christa Pike asked 'Where am I?' after waking up following botched execution: Lawyer Oct 7 The disembarked guests have all been contacted by Oceanwide Expeditions. In the U.S., local authorities in five states -- Arizona, California, Georgia, Texas and Virginia -- are monitoring the disembarked passengers and are conducting contact tracing, None have shown signs of illness at this time. Anais Legend, technical lead for viral hemorrhagic fevers at WHO, said during the press conference on Thursday that "step-by-step guidance is being developed" for the disembarked passengers and that the WHO is coordinating with national authorities. Anyone with any signs of symptoms will be isolated while other passengers have their risk exposure evaluated. The cruise ship MV Hondius, carrying passengers suspected of having cases of hantavirus on board, leaves Praia, Cape Verde, May 6, 2026. Reuters Public health experts said they expected a more robust response from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the National Institutes of Health. "CDC would typically be asked by WHO to, or by a country to, help in technical assistance," Dr. Carlos del Rio, an H. Cliff Sauls distinguished professor of medicine at the Emory University School of Medicine, told reporters on Thursday. Typically, CDC teams would be deployed to an area, he said, and the teams would perform contact tracing and interviews and conduct an outbreak investigation. "I would envision by now, many, many days ago, we would have seen ... a team from CDC deployed to the area," he added. Related 3 dead in suspected hantavirus outbreak aboard a cruise ship: What to know Dr. Jeanne Marrazzo, CEO of the IDSA, added that she would have expected a CDC press briefing, an alert from the agency's Health Alert Network or information from the NIH on potential treatments in the pipeline that could receive emergency use authorization to help treat hantavirus patients. Marrazzo said she is not aware that conversations about potential therapies at NIH aren't happening but it "does not give me a lot of assurance or reassurance that we're not hearing about any of it." The CDC posted a statement on X on Wednesday on behalf of NIH Director and acting CDC director Dr. Jay Bhattacharya that read, "Our hearts go out to the passengers aboard the cruise ship M/V Hondius and their families during this difficult time. Our CDC team began coordinating with domestic and international partners as soon as we were notified of a hantavirus situation." The statement said there is "clear, written health guidance to the American passengers through the State Department" and that the CDC "will continue to update as more information becomes available and remains committed to protecting the health and safety of the American public." The agency also published a statement on its website stating that the Trump administration "is closely monitoring the situation" and that the Department of State "is leading a coordinated, whole-of-government response including direct contact with passengers, diplomatic coordination, and engagement with domestic and international health authorities." The CDC also said the risk to the American public is "extremely low." The WHO said during Thursday's press briefing that the U.S. is coordinating with the global health agency in a technical capacity. Because the cluster is limited and confined to a cruise ship, the "idea of sending messages across the world and panicking everyone is not required," said Dr. Abdirahman Mahmoud, director of the WHO's health emergency alert and response operations. He added that the WHO is "informally" aware that contact tracing has been done of the U.S. passengers who disembarked last month and are back home. supplementary_news.content: Report Timeframe (link is external) : September 24-September 30, 2026. Current Vermont Department of Health recommendations on preventing COVID-19 (link is external) by Timothy McQuiston, Vermont Business Magazine The Vermont Department of Health has reported that COVID-19 hospitalizations remain scarce. However, the COVID-19 virus (SARS-CoV-2) remains active in Vermont at the Montpelier, Essex Junction and South Burlington test sites. It is also being found across the nation. Meanwhile, Norovirus and EVD68 have become more pronounced. There was one COVID outbreak reported at a long-term care facility in Bennington County. Enterovirus D68 (EV-D68) is a virus that causes respiratory illness similar to the common cold (link is external) . It sometimes leads to severe breathing issues and outbreaks of neurological disease (acute flaccid myelitis) that causes paralysis. Most people regain some muscle function, but some may have lasting health issues. See most recent test results below. Neither the VDH nor the CDC are any longer reporting COVID fatalities or total cases in Vermont or in the US. The hospitalizations dataset contains day-level data reported from all Vermont hospitals each Tuesday. Reported numbers are subject to correction. Laboratory-confirmed and diagnosed COVID-19 cases and COVID-19 outbreaks must still be reported to the Vermont Department of Health. There was 1 COVID outbreak last week (1 the week before), with 1 in Long-Term Care Facilities and 0 in schools. Outbreaks had disappeared since mid-summer. There have been no school outbreaks even as students have returned to the classroom. Overall, there have been only 5 outbreaks, all in LTC, since the March 2, 2026, report. supplementary_news.content: ‌ ‌ Skip to main content Cork Beo - Latest Cork news, sport & opinion News Crime Cork City Cork Loves More News Latest News Local News Crime Jobs Cork City County Cork Gardai Weather Traffic History Culture Best of Cork Food & Drink Music & Nightlife Family & Kids What's On News Cork Loves Property Sport Soccer GAA Rugby Business Travel Partner Stories CLOSE Local News Cork City Munster Newsletter Signup Cork Loves Property Advertise With Us News Latest News Local News Crime Jobs Cork City County Cork Gardai Weather Traffic History Culture Best of Cork Food & Drink Music & Nightlife Family & Kids What's On News Cork Loves Property Sport Soccer GAA Rugby Business Travel Partner Stories Local News Cork City Munster Newsletter Signup Cork Loves Property Advertise With Us News Coronavirus New 'American Covid' strain sees surge of cases across Ireland Experts say the strain has one distinctive symptom Add to preferred sources News Neil James Shaw, Daire Fitton Senior Reporter and Neil Shaw 14:23, 08 Oct 2026 View Image A woman squeezing the sample liquid on a test strip while carrying out a Covid-19 rapid self test at home. As the cold August weather rolls in, there's been a notable rise in Covid cases here in Ireland - and experts say a new' variant dubbed XFG or American Covid is to blame. ‌ ‌ This strain was discovered in 2025 and was named American Covid after it rapidly became the dominant strain across the United States last year. Now, it's responsible for 55% of cases here in Ireland, and experts say the variant appears to have one prominent symptom that could help you identify it. ‌ The Health Protection Surveillance Centre is monitoring infection rates and has confirmed that hundreds of new Covid cases are now being recorded in Ireland each week, leading to dozens of hospitalisations. ‌ Dr Bruno Silvester Lopes, lecturer in microbiology at Teesside University, said the XFG variant is "linked to hoarseness and fatigue". Many people with Covid now report a hoarse voice or a 'scratchy' throat. Pharmacist Daniel Cheung, writing in NowPatient, said: "The key symptoms and most noticeable symptoms of the Stratus variant include hoarseness, scratchy/raspy voice, which is considered a unique symptom distinguishing it from other Covid strains." He said other symptoms include a dry cough, sore throat, fever, fatigue, muscle aches and a loss of sense of taste and smell. ‌ GP Dr Renée Hoenderkamp told the Mail patients with Covid now complain of sore throats, headaches, runny noses and fatigue. She said: "In the past 10 days to three weeks in general practice, my lists have definitely changed to people with these symptoms." Dr Hoenderkamp added: "It's very flu‐like, actually, which is probably the fairest way to describe it." One woman who recently had Covid explained her symptoms, saying: "I was absolutely exhausted, with a temperature, cough and really painful flu-like aches in my legs and joints. There were times in the morning when I'd think: 'I'm fine, get your act together', but by lunchtime I'd have to go back to bed. I slept through a lot of it." She said her daughter 'had a really bad headache, sore throat and cough, a raging temperature and was completely exhausted'. Her GP said they had seen three patients with similar symptoms that day. ‌ GP Dr Saira Bano, founder of SwiftDoctor, said: "A loss or change in your sense of taste or smell is still a recognised Covid symptom, but it isn't the giveaway sign people may remember from earlier in the pandemic. It became much less common with Omicron compared with earlier variants, and an ordinary cold can also reduce your sense of smell, particularly if your nose is badly congested. "So a change in taste or smell shouldn't automatically be taken to mean you have Covid. Nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea can also occur with Covid and other respiratory viral infections, but they aren't the dominant symptoms you'd normally expect with a straightforward cold. If vomiting and diarrhoea are the main problem, I'd also consider a stomach infection such as norovirus rather than immediately assuming it's flu or Covid." If you take a test and test positive, the HSE says you should stay at home and avoid contact with other people for five days. The advice reads: "You can leave home after 5 days if your symptoms have fully or mostly gone for the last 48 hours." Article continues below You should also avoid meeting people who are at very high risk for 10 days. This starts from the day you first had symptoms. ENJOYED THIS STORY? Share Article Share Article Facebook X LinkedIn Reddit Bluesky Email Copy Link Link copied Bookmark Add us as preferred source 4 Comments By Laura Zilincanova 16:00, Thu, Oct 8, 2026 Health experts have issued advice on whether Britons should start wearing face masks again as a rise in Covid infections and hospital admissions sparks concern over the so-called 'American Covid' variant. The strain, officially known as XFG or Stratus, emerged in early 2025 and is a combination of two Omicron descendants, LF.7 and LP.8.1.2. American Covid is its media nickname as the variant continues to spread in the US. Figures show that Covid hospital admissions in England have risen by approximately 48%, although overall infection levels remain low. However, it remains the most common current variant. Masks are not routinely required but can help reduce the risk of catching or spreading infection, particularly in crowded indoor spaces or around vulnerable people. "A well-fitting FFP2 mask offers better personal protection than a loose-fitting face covering. However, masks do not eliminate the risk, so anyone with COVID symptoms should avoid close contact with others where possible." Dr Bruno Silvester Lopes, Senior Lecturer in Microbiology at Teesside University, added that masks can help people with weakened immune systems. Both experts stressed that XFG does not appear to cause more severe illness than other circulating variants. Common symptoms include coughing, fever, fatigue and body aches. Some patients have also reported particularly sore, scratchy or hoarse throats. Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT Dr Siggins added that these throat symptoms have not been proved unique to XFG. He advised people with Covid symptoms to avoid visiting vulnerable relatives while unwell, adding that waiting around 10 days after symptoms begin is a sensible precaution. Dr Alex Allen, Consultant Epidemiologist at the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), said: "The strains currently going around, including those known as XFG, are closely related to strains that have been with us for over a year, so this isn't something new. "We're also not seeing any evidence that these are making people more ill or spreading faster than before, and this year's autumn vaccine has been specifically designed to protect against them." Dr Allen urged eligible people to get vaccinated, saying: "Don't risk it, get the vaccine and give yourself the best protection." Cases are on the rise in the UK, with words like "XFG" and "American covid" frequently popping up on the news- but what exactly does this mean? XFG is a variant of Covid-19, often referred to as the Stratus variant or also "American covid". It remains the most common Covid-19 variant. Despite different warnings shared in the media, it is not new and has been circulating in the UK and other countries for around a year. UKHSA data shows that Covid-19 positive test rates rose to around 7% in September, with hospital admission rates increasing by approximately 50% over the same period. A statement shared by UKHSA said: "As increases in hospitalisations are rising in line with overall increases in Covid-19 circulation - rather than rising sharply on their own - this suggests a general increase in Covid-19 activity rather than a variant causing more severe disease." Advice added: "If you have symptoms of a respiratory infection, such as Covid-19, and you have a high temperature or do not feel well enough to go to work or carry out normal activities, you should avoid contact with vulnerable people and stay at home if possible." To reduce the chance of passing your infection onto others, you can wear a face mask, avoid crowded places like public transport and cover your mouth and nose when you cough or sneeze. Symptoms of XFG are similar to other variants of Covid-19 like Delta and Omicron. It can cause a sore throat, fever and cough. Other symptoms to look out for include a high temperature, shortness of breath, a loss or change in sense of smell or taste and feeling sick or being sick. RESPIRATORY viruses showed distinct links to pneumonia, bronchiolitis, and airway exacerbations, while collectively tracking hospital admissions. A study of 1,801 hospital admissions for acute respiratory infections found that influenza A, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), and human rhinovirus (HRV) showed different associations with major respiratory presentations. However, overall respiratory virus circulation showed the strongest temporal relationship with hospital admission patterns. Researchers analyzed admissions between November 2019 and March 2020, before the emergence of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2. Patients were classified as having pneumonia, bronchiolitis, or reactive airway exacerbations, while respiratory samples were tested for influenza A and other common respiratory viruses. Influenza A was most strongly represented among patients admitted with pneumonia. Of patients with influenza A alone, 76.5% were in the pneumonia group. The influenza A wave peaked during epidemiological week 5 of 2020, when it accounted for 33% of infections tested. Other respiratory viruses were more prominent in bronchiolitis and reactive airway exacerbations. RSV was the main virus associated with bronchiolitis, particularly among infants, while HRV was the most common viral trigger identified in acute exacerbations of asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Infants younger than 1 year accounted for more than 90% of bronchiolitis admissions associated with influenza A testing, and age emerged as one of the strongest determinants of clinical presentation. Although individual respiratory viruses showed preferential associations with particular conditions, no virus was confined to a single presentation. Viral co-infections were also uncommon. When researchers combined activity from all respiratory viruses, viral circulation was strongly correlated with hospital admissions, with a correlation coefficient of 0.88. This relationship was stronger than patterns observed for individual pathogens, suggesting that the collective burden of circulating respiratory viruses may better reflect seasonal demand on hospital services. Air quality measures, including ozone, sulfur dioxide, nitrogen dioxide, carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxide, and fine particulate matter, did not show consistent independent associations with acute respiratory infection admissions after full adjustment. The researchers noted that the relatively short five month study period and weekly averaging of air quality measurements limited interpretation of environmental effects. Potential diagnostic overlap between bronchiolitis and viral pneumonia in young children was another limitation. Overall, the findings suggest that age and viral type help shape acute respiratory presentations, while combined respiratory virus circulation may provide a broader indication of seasonal hospital burden. Reference Husein M et al. Influenza A and other respiratory viruses show distinct associations with acute respiratory presentations and temporal correlation with hospital admissions. J Med Microbiol. 2026;75(9):002203.
